Remote Rendering Client/Server Architecture separates the volume rendering engine into a server and a client connected via a network, allowing rendering computation to be performed on a remote machine while the user interacts locally [S1][S2, S3, unofficial].

The claim states that Remote Rendering Client/Server Architecture separates the volume rendering engine into a server and a client connected via a network, allowing rendering computation to be performed on a remote machine while the user interacts locally. Source [S1] explicitly describes an architecture that 'strictly separates to individual objects... The engine should be just divided in server and client parts... The server receives commands... and executes the corresponding calls... Results... sent back over the network to the client.' It further notes that 'users work on inexpensive workstations and rendering is done on special dedicated server' and 'the client transparently encodes function calls... used as if all the computing was done locally.' Source [S2] supports this with a 'thin client' approach where 'data is only stored at a remote rendering server, and all rendering and compositing occurs remotely. The client only receives final, composited RGB images... and the client supports a user interface to select rendering parameters and interactively change viewpoints.' Source [S3] also describes remote clients establishing network connections to remote servers that own renderers. All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
